Vukani Aviation Academy

By: Diana Lucas | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A pilot training project which is not teaching pilots to fly our friendly skies

Summary:
The South African Flight Training Academy was granted R77 million from government to train licensed commercial pilots, money granted to Nhlahla Dube who styles himself as a former ‘Commander of the Presidential Jet’.

When Dube’s company, Vukani Aviation, was awarded the contract to lead the National Skills Fund's "New Growth Path" project to train 59 new pilots from disadvantaged backgrounds, it was a surprise. At that point he didn’t have an aviation school and had to buy one.

In addition to the NSF allocation of R66 million, Dube also received R12 million from the Transport Education and Training Authority (Teta) to train another 12 pilots.

There are allegations that this project, which charges R1.2 million per pilot (far more than other aviation schools charge) is nothing more than a get rich scheme for Dube. The first thing he did when awarded the project was buy himself a helicopter and a Porsche, which he hides in the Kruger Park Airfield when there are Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) checks, according to his students.

The CAA has confirmed a probe into SAFTA (South African Flight Training Academy).

The probe follows several complaints about management of the flight academy in Heidelberg, Gauteng, as well as questions about the "lucrative" R1.2-million-per-pilot programme.

CAA spokesperson Sandy Motale said an audit of Dube's school last week had found operations to be "unacceptable".

Despite the massive cash injection, only a third of the cadets have obtained their commercial pilot's licence almost two years after the first cadet intake.
In addition not a single cadet has been employed at either of the two national carriers, South African Airways and SA Express - a key programme objective.


Further information:
SAA spokesman Tlali Tlali this week confirmed that the airline had "not absorbed any cadets or pilots trained at his school".

Rival flying schools claim the move undermines the vital need to transform aviation - a move supported by the private aviation industry and considered a government priority.

The Department of Higher Education, spokesman Khaye Nkwanyana said a similar contract had been awarded to Deloitte Consulting Services in 2012, worth R78-million. Not true - only R 8 million went into the Deloitte pilot programme and furthermore the Deloitte pilot programme produced 16 fully qualified commercial pilots within two years. By comparison Dube's school has so far received almost 10 times as much with only limited results.

Other queries and allegations that have emerged:

- Dube was never commander of the presidential jet, as advertised on his company website. The air force confirmed he was an ordinary pilot.
- At the time the NSF allocation was made Dube had no flight school. Was it his political connections that trumped funding applications from other established flight schools who have been training disadvantaged pilots for years?;
- After Dube took over, the school lost several flight instructors, including some who left due to fears over maintenance and pilot safety. He also fired instructors replacing them with fewer and far less experienced ones.
- Students have signed dubious contracts with the school and been misled into what their training would entail. Those who complain said he has threatened them
- There are only a handful of working planes, which are not being maintained. There have been numerous recent mechanical "mishaps" and training "incidents" at Dube's school, including tools being left inside an aircraft engine and problems with the school's flight simulator. A plane recently crash-landed into a vegetable field next door to the airfield.
Dube has countered the allegations and criticisms saying these people oppose transformation.

"When we took over, Safta did not even have a single black instructor. Today there are more than five black instructors. But because there are black instructors the standard has dropped?"

He also maintains the average cost of R1.2-million per student was due to Safta's extensive training that went way beyond normal flight training: "Safta is not only training cadets to do 200 hours [flying] like all the other schools. We go way beyond that."

This is an outrage. On the one hand you have disadvantaged, young, bright people, cadet pilots whose training has been less than adequate so their chance at improving their future has been compromised. On the other hand you have the National Skills Fund, becoming a ‘slush’ fund for the politically connected. Despite complaints and calls for investigation nothing has been done and the students have been grounded. The Department says it is evaluating the situation.

In the current circumstances, the trainee pilots risk not completing their training at all, or completing it but finding their qualification tainted by the current reputation of the Vukani project and SAFTA. They deserve better and so do we.

Press Release:


Vukani Aviation Program
The National Skills Fund has injected R77-million into Vukani Aviation, a flight training program for young pilots from disadvantaged backgrounds. But, it seems the venture hasn’t quite taken off. From a cadet pilot lost above the clouds for over 2 hours without a working radar transponder, to another crash-landing in a mielie field, shocking stories have emerged of compromised safety and critical maintenance shortcuts on aircraft. Carte Blanche asks: why has the Vukani Aviation Program nose-dived?
Producer: Diana Lucas



Script:




LiNK
The pilot of a plane flying illegally at night gets lost

Cadet: It was my first flight and he says, come for a joy flight ride it was at night flying without a night rating.

A cadet gets lost above clouds for over two hours, and the basic navigational equipment isn’t working.

Belinda: She phoned Search and Rescue and was unable to identify land marks on the ground finally found landed at Bara didn’t have working transponder

A passenger jet on its final approach into OR Tambo reports a small plane going overhead.

CFI: All the experienced instructors have left now got essentially the blind leading the blind and they are all taking a short cut straight across the final approach of OR Tambo. it takes one guy a Cessna can take out a massive plane,

LINK
A plane nearly landing on the N3, another one crashing into a mielie field These are just a few of numerous incidents said to emanate from a flight training school in Heidelberg.

V/O 16 sec
The South African Flight Training Academy was one of the most established flight schools in the country when it was bought by Vukani Aviation in 2013. Nhlanhla Dube one of the owners of Vukani had just sealed the deal on a huge empowerment pilot programme

Derek: How much money was given to Dube or Vukani aviation?
Eubert: The contract was originally 78 million which came down to 77 million

V/O 17 sec
Eubert Mashabane is a Director at the National Skills Fund, which aims to upskill disadvantaged people. The Vukani project set to train 43 young men and women to get their commercial pilots licenses and 16 cadets their advanced jet rating
The National Skills Fund falls under the Department of Higher Education and training.

Derek: It was calculated at 1.2 million per pilot, which is far more than any other flying school?

Eubert I agree but were talking about a group of disadvantaged youngsters who had to be recruited into the programme. But over and above that we also cover other costs that your other school don’t cover, like their accommodations and stipends.

V/O 8 and a half sec
But for the publisher of SA flyer, Guy Leitch who has been in the aviation industry for the last 40 years this doesn’t hold water:

Guy: It seems extraordinarily inefficient it should cost between ½ a million and 700 thousand rand to develop these pilot even if you are paying full board and lodging, it would indicate that they are charging almost twice the normal going rate.

LINK
Eventually about 60 wanna be pilots were selected for the programme. They came from all parts of the country from al walks of life….and some gave up the opportunity of other promising careers of university degrees.

V/O 6 and a half sec
We spoke to a group of cadets, three of them bravely agreed to talk to us anonymously on camera.

Cadet: It was a golden opportunity, to be sponsored for such a huge amount.
Derek: What was it like when you got that call back?
Cadet: So exciting then and there I knew my dream has come true.

V/O 13 sec
In 2013 the Vukani pilot programme was airborne. It started well,
But for a former Chief Flying instructor, who has asked to remain anonymous, the maintenance of the planes then began to be questionable.

CFI We started seeing these little snags wont being and fixed some parts from a plane when it was in for maintenance were put into another plane to make it look like it was.

V/O 7 and a half
The loss of some of mechanics and avionics engineers affected, Nancy Raphela, the avionics apprentice.

Nancy: Whenever the CAA came they would tell them they on leave we were also told if they asked we must say this person is on leave so we went by that.
Derek: So when there were inspections you were told to say people were on leave
Nancy Exactly.


V/0 4 sec
And then, according to Nancy, she was often working without supervision.

Nancy:….. the guy who was working on fuel bay left the guy who was working in stores left.my engineer avionicsngineer who was teaching me also left then not only was I the only avionic person left I had to go and fix the planes sometimes I wouldn’t know what to do I would just go and try and figure out something most of the time funnily enough it worked I would get things working, I don’t know how.
Derek: So you were lucky enough to fix the problem
Nancy: Most of the time yes.
Derek: But without a qualified avionics engineer?
Nancy: There was no qualified avionics engineer at the time
but the AME would come now and again to check, he is allowed to over sign me so he would come and check and say if you don’t know just leave it because there is nothing I can do because there is no avionics engineer those people have to hire somebody.


V/O 10 sec
The cadets claim they were forced to fly in bad weather, radio failures, aeroplanes stuck together with sticky tape, transponders not working and braking problems

Cadet:… And as I landed the brakes didn’t work and when I came to report the brake failure he said no fine don’t fill in any documents
Cadet: Yes, it’s been a trend of theirs not to keep written evidence of things that’s when audits and assessments and when we make such claims they cant find the evidence anywhere at all.

V/O 4
We gave Nhlanhla Dube, the right of reply to the allegations

Derek; Why training cadets with aircraft that have not been maintained properly and are unsafe?
Dube All aeroplanes are certified by the CAA so they come here all the time to check our aeroplanes , check if they are safe to fly and they give them a certificate to say this aircraft is airworthy.
Derek We are told when the CAA inspectors came around aircraft were hidden from them and your staff were told to lie about engineers being on leave.
Dube: I have never heard of that, do not take disgruntled black students who are aggrieved because and bring it to me.
Derek; But you have got an apprentice mechanic saying I dint really know what I was doing but I got it right most of the time?
Dube: It can never be anything like that definitely she was lying.

V/O 5 sec
According to the cadets, in the beginning they approached Dube about their concerns.

Cadet: In our first weeks when we raised concern regarding safety we were told that you broke my aircraft but we as students we know for a fact we did not break anything of his. There is always blame shifted on to his students

Dube: A certain number from the group started non performing now as a school we not going to compromise safety and when those students were told to leave they became disgruntled. And they were running to the media to do all sorts of things to try and stay within the school.
Derek: How can you say to me they are all disgruntled failed students that is not true?
Dube: What I am saying to you that is what I know>
Derek That is a broad brush over all these problems

V/O
It has to be an extreme situation when a group of trainee pilots, anxious to get their commercial licenses refuse to continue with flying lessons.

Cadet: Obviously we realised the importance of getting done with qualifications asap but when factors of safety are present you don’t have a choice but to blow the whistle.

V/O 8 sec
The cadets took their concerns to the DA’s shadow Minister for Higher Education and Training, Belinda Bozzoli.

Belinda: I first brought it to the attention of the Director General of the Department about asking him to act quickly he responded and said he would institute an enquiry into the school but that then took a long time in coming so that was when I first raised it in parliament I decided this was taking too long students lives were definitely at risk

V/O
It was In August, when Belinda called for the programme to be halted and the cadets relocated to other flying schools. … two weeks ago finally the National Skills Fund initiated an assessment.

Derek: What do you think of this revolt by some of the students?
CFI: I take my hat off to them to take on some one like Col Dube, I think it should have happened a good year or so ago already but I think in the last little bit its got quiet bad there.

LINK
So how do the Directors of the Skills Fund feel about the millions they have injected into the flight programme…and the claims made by some of the students.

Derek: After spending 77 million you have a group of pilots anxious to get their license who refuse to fly because the aircraft are not serviceable?
Eubert: At the time we took this decision there were sufficient aircraft that were in good condition to be able to execute the project. There are challenges at the schools that can be addressed.
Derek: There are challenges I think there are a lot of challenges. You’ve made a recent assessment of the flying school where is that report?
Eubert: That report is still being considered by the department I don’t want to speculate that SAFTA and Vukani have forced students to fly in aircraft that’s unsafe because I don’t have the report especially from the CAA.

LINK
Now that’s a good question. Where were the CAA in keeping a close check on the school, especially after a string of incidents. We asked for an interview but they were not forthcoming.

Guy It’s the Civil Aviation Authority’s job to set the standards and to rigorously maintain them certainly hard questions need to be asked what is going on in terms of the CAA’s oversight in this particular training school

Derek: Derek Weve asked to see the financials why cant you show us how the NSF money was spent?
Dube We cant show you the money
Derek Why
Dube This is a private company
Derek: Why its public money
Dube Its public money yes go the government, why is the government because there is no money that was stolen, I am angry with governemnet don’t know why they wont show you
Derek You don’t look that angry,
Dune Nooo

LINK
So with the assessment still to pass through the hands of the top brass, the students grounded. Where does it leave the flight programme and the futures of so many young people.

Eubert: Our primary goal are these people who we are spending money on. We want to see them to the finish.

Cadet: We want to see this programme as the best because all eyes are on this programme we want to make it work.

CFI: I take my hat off to them to take on some one like Col Dube, I think it should have happened a good year or so ago already but I think in the last little bit its got quiet bad there. LINK So how do the Directors of the Skills Fund feel about the millions they have injected into the flight programme…and the claims made by some of the students. Derek: After spending 77 million you have a group of pilots anxious to get their license who refuse to fly because the aircraft are not serviceable? Eubert: At the time we took this decision there were sufficient aircraft that were in good condition to be able to execute the project. There are challenges at the schools that can be addressed. Derek: There are challenges I think there are a lot of challenges. You’ve made a recent assessment of the flying school where is that report? Eubert: That report is still being considered by the department I don’t want to speculate that SAFTA and Vukani have forced students to fly in aircraft that’s unsafe because I don’t have the report especially from the CAA. LINK Now that’s a good question. Where were the CAA in keeping a close check on the school, especially after a string of incidents. We asked for an interview but they were not forthcoming. Guy It’s the Civil Aviation Authority’s job to set the standards and to rigorously maintain them certainly hard questions need to be asked what is going on in terms of the CAA’s oversight in this particular training school Derek: Derek Weve asked to see the financials why cant you show us how the NSF money was spent? Dube We cant show you the money Derek Why Dube This is a private company Derek: Why its public money Dube Its public money yes go the government, why is the government because there is no money that was stolen, I am angry with governemnet don’t know why they wont show you Derek You don’t look that angry, Dune Nooo LINK So with the assessment still to pass through the hands of the top brass, the students grounded. Where does it leave the flight programme and the futures of so many young people. Eubert: Our primary goal are these people who we are spending money on. We want to see them to the finish. Cadet: We want to see this programme as the best because all eyes are on this programme we want to make it work.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A pilot training project which is not teaching pilots to fly our friendly skies
metadata.Summary: The South African Flight Training Academy was granted R77 million from government to train licensed commercial pilots, money granted to Nhlahla Dube who styles himself as a former ‘Commander of the Presidential Jet’. When Dube’s company, Vukani Aviation, was awarded the contract to lead the National Skills Fund's "New Growth Path" project to train 59 new pilots from disadvantaged backgrounds, it was a surprise. At that point he didn’t have an aviation school and had to buy one. In addition to the NSF allocation of R66 million, Dube also received R12 million from the Transport Education and Training Authority (Teta) to train another 12 pilots. There are allegations that this project, which charges R1.2 million per pilot (far more than other aviation schools charge) is nothing more than a get rich scheme for Dube. The first thing he did when awarded the project was buy himself a helicopter and a Porsche, which he hides in the Kruger Park Airfield when there are Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) checks, according to his students. The CAA has confirmed a probe into SAFTA (South African Flight Training Academy). The probe follows several complaints about management of the flight academy in Heidelberg, Gauteng, as well as questions about the "lucrative" R1.2-million-per-pilot programme. CAA spokesperson Sandy Motale said an audit of Dube's school last week had found operations to be "unacceptable". Despite the massive cash injection, only a third of the cadets have obtained their commercial pilot's licence almost two years after the first cadet intake. In addition not a single cadet has been employed at either of the two national carriers, South African Airways and SA Express - a key programme objective.
metadata.Further information: SAA spokesman Tlali Tlali this week confirmed that the airline had "not absorbed any cadets or pilots trained at his school". Rival flying schools claim the move undermines the vital need to transform aviation - a move supported by the private aviation industry and considered a government priority. The Department of Higher Education, spokesman Khaye Nkwanyana said a similar contract had been awarded to Deloitte Consulting Services in 2012, worth R78-million. Not true - only R 8 million went into the Deloitte pilot programme and furthermore the Deloitte pilot programme produced 16 fully qualified commercial pilots within two years. By comparison Dube's school has so far received almost 10 times as much with only limited results. Other queries and allegations that have emerged: - Dube was never commander of the presidential jet, as advertised on his company website. The air force confirmed he was an ordinary pilot. - At the time the NSF allocation was made Dube had no flight school. Was it his political connections that trumped funding applications from other established flight schools who have been training disadvantaged pilots for years?; - After Dube took over, the school lost several flight instructors, including some who left due to fears over maintenance and pilot safety. He also fired instructors replacing them with fewer and far less experienced ones. - Students have signed dubious contracts with the school and been misled into what their training would entail. Those who complain said he has threatened them - There are only a handful of working planes, which are not being maintained. There have been numerous recent mechanical "mishaps" and training "incidents" at Dube's school, including tools being left inside an aircraft engine and problems with the school's flight simulator. A plane recently crash-landed into a vegetable field next door to the airfield. Dube has countered the allegations and criticisms saying these people oppose transformation. "When we took over, Safta did not even have a single black instructor. Today there are more than five black instructors. But because there are black instructors the standard has dropped?" He also maintains the average cost of R1.2-million per student was due to Safta's extensive training that went way beyond normal flight training: "Safta is not only training cadets to do 200 hours [flying] like all the other schools. We go way beyond that." This is an outrage. On the one hand you have disadvantaged, young, bright people, cadet pilots whose training has been less than adequate so their chance at improving their future has been compromised. On the other hand you have the National Skills Fund, becoming a ‘slush’ fund for the politically connected. Despite complaints and calls for investigation nothing has been done and the students have been grounded. The Department says it is evaluating the situation. In the current circumstances, the trainee pilots risk not completing their training at all, or completing it but finding their qualification tainted by the current reputation of the Vukani project and SAFTA. They deserve better and so do we.
